Even if, as the majority opinion says, the acts of the Defendants were a “many persons” combination sufficient to commit a riot under Article 87, once the Defendants committed murder, they would constitute only one offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88, and would not correspond to attempted insurrection under Article 87. Yet the lower court held that they also correspond to attempted insurrection under Article 87 and that the two offenses were in imaginary concurrence. This cannot be said to be proper. If the lower court’s theory were followed, then a person who caused death by injury would have to be in imaginary concurrence between assault and bodily injury causing death, and a person who committed robbery murder would have to be punished as an imaginary concurrence of robbery and robbery murder. That is the consequence of the lower court’s theory.

2. There is no evidence that the acts of Defendants E, F, and G correspond to murder with insurrectionary purpose.

The crime of insurrection is a crime whose protected legal interest is the existence of the State. To have insurrectionary purpose, there must be a purpose to unlawfully destroy or transform the democratic basic order of Korea. We examine whether these three Defendants, as a subjective requirement, knew that A and others had such purpose and participated in the criminal acts.

As to Defendants E and F, they were told only by Defendant D, as instructed by the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, that if gunshots were heard inside, they should drive the Blue House security guards to one side, and if those guards tried to shoot, they should shoot back. They merely carried that out. They never heard that the President was to be shot, and Defendants E and F did not know what the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency was doing inside. It cannot be said that they participated while knowing that A and others had the purpose of subverting the Constitution. To recognize a criminal fact there must be strict proof, and one cannot infer that these Defendants also had insurrectionary purpose merely by conjecture.

Moreover, Defendant G was on guard in a building separated from the building where the incident occurred and did not know what had happened there. Later, at the instruction of Defendants D and E, he performed the confirmation killing on three or four of the victims who had been shot and fallen down, without knowing who those victims were or why they had been shot. Defendant G was told by Defendant E that the President, Chief Secretary C, and the Central Intelligence Agency director had already escaped from the scene, and then he performed the confirmation killing. What evidence supports that Defendant G had insurrectionary purpose? No such evidence appears in the record.

Also, the so-called confirmation killing by Defendant G took place after a considerable time had passed since the occurrence, and even according to the evidence appearing in the record, it is not clear whether Defendant G fired at already dead bodies or at victims before death. The hearing on this point cannot be said to have been fully conducted.

3. There is no evidence that Defendant C conspired with Defendant A, who killed T, as a conspiracy co-principal.

In general, it is beyond dispute that a person who participates in a conspiracy or plot to commit a crime cannot escape co-principal liability for the criminal acts executed by other conspirators even if he does not directly participate in the execution. But the lower court and the majority opinion have misunderstood the law of conspiracy co-principal liability, confusing or equating the elements of execution co-principal liability and conspiracy co-principal liability, or making evidentiary judgments contrary to logic and experience.

That is, in execution co-principal liability, a conspiracy may exist if there is an agreement in the broad sense such as “common awareness of joint crime” or “communication of intent.” But for conspiracy co-principal liability to be recognized, such broad agreement is insufficient; there must be a higher-level agreement approaching indirect perpetration.

Therefore, conspiracy or plot in conspiracy co-principal liability must be strictly construed as existing only where there is a “high-level plot” among two or more persons to become one with a shared intent for a specific crime, using each other’s acts to carry out their own intent. For conspiracy co-principal liability to be recognized, the following additional requirements must be met:
(1) such high-level conspiracy or plot among several persons,
(2) one of them must have carried out the planned offense,
(3) the execution of the crime must have been caused by the conspiracy or plot under item (1).

Thus, we must determine from the evidence in the record:
① whether Defendant C and A made a sufficiently high-level agreement to kill T as described above;
② whether A killed T because of the conspiracy with C, that is, whether A killed T because of the agreement with C to kill him.

The lower court and the majority opinion cite as evidence A’s statement to the military prosecutor that, while sitting on the curb in the garden in front of the restaurant, when A said to C around 17:50 that “Shall I get rid of that guy” referring to T, he looked at C’s expression and C nodded his head, and that when he said “Please take care of what happens after this,” C nodded again. They also rely on similar statements by Defendant C. But A said in the first-instance court that he never told the prosecutor that C nodded when he said that, and that he only said C appeared to nod. A further stated that when he sat with C on the curb and casually said, “Shall I get rid of T?”, he thought C would understand it as simply making T look bad, and he did not think C would imagine that T would be shot in front of the President. C also stated that he was not the kind of person who would agree with A’s actions and participate in them. At the first-instance court, C stated that while waiting for the President’s arrival in the restaurant garden, he never heard words about getting rid of T or about taking care of the aftermath, and that A had often previously used the expression “get rid of him” about T. Thus, the prosecutor’s interrogation statement that C nodded when A said “Shall I get rid of T?” is insufficient to establish that fact as it stands. Even if the facts in the prosecutor’s record are accepted as they are, it still cannot be said that the two agreed in the restaurant garden to kill T. That is, A had already firmly resolved to shoot T and the President long before meeting C, and after completing preparations such as checking the pistol upon arriving at the Gungjeong-dong restaurant, he only told C at around 17:40. Then, can we conclude from the short interval while waiting for the President’s arrival that, in the garden in front of the restaurant, an agreement to kill the President’s security chief was formed through a casual “shall we get rid of him” and a nod? The prosecutor’s statement alone does not support that A and C became one in order to kill T, with C using A’s act to carry out C’s own resolution to kill T.

Furthermore, for conspiracy co-principal liability to be recognized, the third requirement above must be met, namely that A’s act of killing T was carried out because of the conspiracy with C. Can A’s act really be seen as having been carried out pursuant to a conspiracy with C and as executing the content of the conspiracy? A did not execute a conspiratorial plan with C; rather, he had already fully fixed his intent before meeting C and then killed T pursuant to that intent, which is a clear fact on the record. Thus, C cannot be a conspiracy co-principal in the killing of T from that point of view either.

Not only that, but all evidence in the record lacks even the material to show the high-level agreement needed for conspiracy co-principal liability between C and A; it is not even enough to say that C knew in advance that A would kill T in front of the President.

In the end, although the lower court and majority opinion seem to accept that because A shot the President and T, the bias from that offense caused them to take A’s “shall I get rid of T?” as meaning he would kill T, and that C understood it that way, the phrase “shall I get rid of T” does not necessarily mean killing T, and given the circumstances that day at the President’s presence, it is far removed from our rules of experience to infer that A’s ambiguous and fragmentary remark meant he would kill T in front of the President. Therefore, Defendant C cannot be regarded as a conspiracy co-principal in T’s killing. Nor can there be said to be communication of intent even in the broader sense, so C cannot be said to have known A would kill T. Even if C had known A would kill T, mere passivity despite knowing another’s crime is not punishable by any provision. In any event, C cannot be regarded as a joint principal who aided in killing T.

As to Defendant C’s attempted insurrection offense, as stated in item 1 above, there was no riot by a combination of many persons using violence or intimidation, so there is no room to apply attempted insurrection to C.

Even if, as the majority opinion says, the acts of the Defendants in this case correspond to a riot under Article 87 of the Criminal Act, the lower court’s conclusion that when A came out after the offense and said to C, “Please keep security,” C responded and that this proves he was a major participant under Article 87(2) of the Criminal Act is a misunderstanding of Article 87(2). If everyone who receives a unilateral request from A to keep security and does not resist is recognized as a major participant in insurrection, then if some persons were also present at the offense scene and A asked them not to tell anyone, and they complied without objection, they too would become major participants in insurrection. That result is untenable.

4. Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act and Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act provide that where the death penalty, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for 10 years or more is imposed, and there is a manifest reason to recognize that the sentence is grossly improper, such can be a ground for appeal. However, Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act does not contain a provision allowing appeal on the ground of excessive sentence. We therefore examine whether civilians, not military personnel or military employees, who were tried by a military court may appeal on the ground of excessive sentence, and whether the right of resistance can be recognized in our country and applied as a judicial norm.

(1) The issue of Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act

As a general question, regardless of whether the sentence in this case against the Defendants was excessive, there is a doubt as to the argument that a person tried by a military court cannot appeal on the ground of excessive sentence, so I note this.

Whereas Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that the above-mentioned heavy sentence may be a ground of appeal, Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act does not contain such a provision among the grounds of appeal, so a person tried by a military court cannot appeal on the ground of excessive sentence. This may be justifiable if the person tried by the military court was a military member or military employee in view of the particularity of that status and service. But if a civilian who is neither military personnel nor military employee is sentenced to such punishment by a military court, there is no distinction from a person tried by an ordinary court, and there is no rational basis to treat them differently. Therefore, depriving them of the right to appeal on the ground of excessive sentence merely because they were tried by a military court cannot be regarded as a rational measure in light of Article 9 of the Constitution, which provides equality before the law. Thus, for civilians who are not military personnel or military employees, even if tried by a military court, there is no reason to distinguish them from those tried by an ordinary court, and it may be interpreted that they can appeal under Article 383 of the Criminal Procedure Act on the ground of excessive sentence. If, however, even civilians must be interpreted as unable to appeal on the ground of excessive sentence under the express language of Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act, then at least as to civilians, there may arise the issue that Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act violates Article 9 of the Constitution.

According to Article 525 of the Military Court-Martial Act, members of the military and military employees tried by a military court in an area under emergency martial law are prohibited from appealing, while civilians who are not military personnel or military employees are not restricted in their right to appeal even if tried by a military court. This shows that, for civilians, even if they were tried by a military court, the right to appeal is not restricted in order to maintain parity with the case of trial in an ordinary court. If Article 432 of the Military Court-Martial Act is interpreted as treating civilians the same as military personnel and military employees, then it is a provision that discriminates against the exercise of civil rights equally guaranteed to anyone.

(2) The issue of the right of resistance

The majority opinion states that it will maintain this Court’s decision dated April 8, 1975, 74DA3323, holding that an argument invoking the right of resistance, an extra-legal concept of right, to justify acts contrary to positive law cannot be accepted. It is not clear whether that precedent denies the existence of the right of resistance itself in Korea or whether it merely means that the right of resistance cannot be applied as a judicial norm. In this case, the acts of Defendant A and others cannot be regarded as an exercise of the right of resistance given the content of the offense, so there is no need to discuss the right of resistance in connection with this case. However, as a general matter, I wish to point out the following doubts as to whether one can deny the existence of the right of resistance in our country or deny its application as a judicial norm.

Where a serious infringement by a state organ is committed against the democratic order centered on human dignity, which is the basic political order of our country, and the majority of the people judge that the existence itself of the democratic constitution is objectively being denied, if there is no way to remedy it by means available under positive law at that time, the people cannot simply watch passively or promote it. In such a case, for the protection of human rights and the basic order of the democratic constitution, the right of resistance consisting of refusal to comply with duties under positive law or to obey positive-law commands that formally appear lawful but substantively violate human rights and the democratic basic order should be recognized as a kind of natural-law right even if not explicitly written into the Constitution. If such a right of resistance is recognized, there is no basis to exclude its function as a judicial norm.

As grounds for denying the existence of such a right of resistance, the Preamble to our Constitution declares that it inherits the spirit of the April 19 democratic movement and ... establishes a new democratic republic; although the events of April 19, viewed under the positive law then in force, were complete criminal acts and unlawful, the Constitution’s Preamble designates them as a revolutionary act and declares inheritance of its spirit. If one evaluates the Preamble legally, one can only interpret it as meaning that our Constitution viewed the April 19 uprising as an exercise of the people’s right of resistance to preserve or defend a democratic order that was being destroyed. One wonders whether a right of resistance recognized by our Constitution can be denied in judicial judgment, and whether, once recognized, there is any rational reason to deprive it of effect by saying it cannot be applied as a judicial norm. The majority opinion states that the right of resistance has no basis in positive law and therefore cannot be applied as a judicial norm. However, there can be no legal principle that natural-law rights can never function as judicial norms, and the above-mentioned Preamble of our Constitution may also be seen as a positive-law basis for the right of resistance.

4. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Kim Yun-haeng

Article 87 of the Criminal Act is the so-called collective offense of insurrection, and “폭동” here means violence or intimidation by a combination of a mob sufficient to disturb the peace of a locality. In this case, taking the view that the acts of the Defendants do not constitute such a mob combination, I share the theory already expressed by Justice Im Hang-jun concerning that the six Defendants A, C, D, E, F, and G, excluding Defendant H, cannot be subject to the crime of insurrection, and also concerning that as to Defendant C, the lower judgment’s finding of conspiracy co-principal liability with A for the killing of T cannot be established.

Further, even if the insurrection (attempt) offenses recognized by the lower court could apply to the Defendants, the lower court recognized as to the remaining Defendants other than Defendant C the relation of imaginary concurrence on the ground that their acts also corresponded to murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88. I point out that this legal application was mistaken for the following reasons.

The reason is that the crime of insurrection takes as its constituent element a riot for the purpose of insurrection, and the riot referred to here is, by virtue of Article 87(2) of the Criminal Act concerning insurrection, broad enough to include “a person who executes an act of killing” as well as one who participates in plotting, directs, or engages in other important duties. Therefore, it is a concept that broadly includes acts from simple violence and intimidation to acts such as murder, injury, and arson. Accordingly, in a riot for insurrectionary purpose, even if someone is killed during the riot process, this constitutes a single insurrection offense, and depending on the position and role forming the group, they are separately punished under Article 87(1) through (3) as leader, participant in plotting, director, major-duty participant, or mere participant. By contrast, Article 88 of the Criminal Act, which defines murder with insurrectionary purpose, only says “a person who kills another for the purpose of insurrection,” which clearly means a case in which a person is killed not by riot but otherwise. Therefore, even if a person kills another for the same insurrectionary purpose, if it is carried out in the course of a riot, it is absorbed into the insurrection offense and becomes only an insurrection offense under Article 87; if it is not carried out by riot, then it is only a single offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88.

If, as the lower court thought, such cases always become imaginary concurrence, then in the case of a leader of insurrection, the statutory penalty is death, life imprisonment, or life imprisonment without labor, and murder with insurrectionary purpose also has the same statutory penalty, so one might say that in the case of the leader there is no practical effect. However, in the case of “a person who executes an act of killing” in the course of riot under insurrection, that person is punished, as noted above, with the same punishment as a conspirator, director, or other important-duty participant, and the penalty is death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for at least 5 years. In some cases, the person could be punished by imprisonment or imprisonment without labor for a fixed term of at least 5 years. By contrast, in imaginary concurrence, Article 40 of the Criminal Act requires punishment according to the heaviest penalty prescribed for the most serious offense, so the person would always be punished by death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment without labor under Article 88, which makes no balance with Article 87(2), which prescribes imprisonment or imprisonment without labor for at least 5 years. (That the penalty for murder with insurrectionary purpose under Article 88 is prescribed as heavier than that under Article 87(2) for “a person who executes an act of killing” in the course of insurrectionary riot is somewhat difficult to understand and not fully balanced, but in insurrection offenses, because mob psychology operates in collective crime and people often act rashly without deep thought, the expectation of compliance is low; thus, I understand the difference in statutory penalties between this and non-riot murder with insurrectionary purpose.) In light of this, in this case the lower court, while describing the acts of Defendants D, E, F, and G as those of persons engaged in important duties in the riot constituting insurrection, nevertheless applied to them the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose and punished them by the heavier penalty of murder with insurrectionary purpose. This amounts to a case where the application of law was wrong and it affected the judgment. Therefore, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that maintains such lower judgment, and the lower judgment should also be reversed on this point.

5. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Jeong Tae-won

This is the same as part (2) of the opinion of Supreme Court Justice Seo Yun-hong below concerning Defendants E and F, and part (3) concerning Defendant G.

6. Opinion of Supreme Court Justice Seo Yun-hong

In view of the facts and evidence in this case, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that would maintain the lower judgment finding all charges against Defendants C, E, F, and G guilty for the following reasons.

(1) As to Defendant C

First, regarding the offense of murder by conspiracy co-principal liability against this Defendant, the point of the lower court (Army High Military Court) in finding this guilty is ultimately that the Defendant conspired with co-defendant A to kill the deceased T, the President’s security chief, and although he did not directly act, he caused A to carry out the killing and thus achieved the purpose. The supporting facts and evidence are summarized as follows: two hours before the shooting as execution of the murder by A (the shooting occurred at 19:40 on October 26, 1979, and the meeting between Defendant and A was at 17:50 on the same day, so less than two hours had passed), when the Defendant met A at the curb in the garden at the entrance to the Gungjeong-dong office, the Blue House branch of the Central Intelligence Agency, A said “I will get rid of the chief T,” and the Defendant nodded; he did not restrain A’s conduct at the shooting scene; and later that day, when the situation developed and Defendant met A in the restroom of the Army Headquarters banka and rebuked him, saying “Why did you even kill the President?”, from these things it was inferred that he intended the gunshot killing of T.

However, the so-called conspiracy co-principal liability is a concept concerning an execution principal. In light of social reality, in crimes by multiple persons there are cases where the substantive principal plans the crime behind the scenes and causes the execution act to be carried out by subordinates or persons under the principal’s control, and in such cases simple instigation or aiding and abetting is not enough. This theory emerged from judicial necessity. Even in such cases, the substantive principal must have the subjective intent to commit the crime as his own. Merely inducing another’s intent or tolerating or using another’s crime does not fall within this category. (The Supreme Court seems already in Decision 57DO380 dated June 12, 1959 to have expressed this through the terms “subject of intent” or “single body of intent,” and the Japanese Supreme Court in Decision of May 28, 1958, Case No. 29(ka)1056, expressly held that subjective intent is required.) In this case, the lower court’s reasoning concerning Defendant C and the supporting facts are plainly not of that nature. No one can deny that the true subject of this shocking offense of assassinating the President was A, not Defendant C, but it is hard to understand that only with respect to the part of killing T the Defendant is treated as the principal and A as the executor under Defendant’s direction. Even if it is true that the Defendant nodded when A said “get rid of him,” that would, at most, mean he tolerated murder, and it is unclear why that can become a joint plot to kill. Likewise, even if he did not restrain A at the scene of the killing, that was merely passivity toward murder. More inexplicable still, the fact that the chief secretary Defendant did not restrain the shooting death of the President at the scene is not reproached in this case, yet failing to restrain the killing of the security chief is treated as conspiracy co-principal liability for murder. Also, the conversation in the Army banka restroom with A as a post hoc support for the plot is hard to accept when the plot itself is a major fact requiring strict proof.

Second, as to the attempted insurrection offense against the same Defendant, insurrection is a crime under Article 87 of the Criminal Act with the purpose of subverting the Constitution, and the concrete content of the Constitution at issue in this case is that the constitutional order was to be changed by assassinating the President. Therefore, whether Defendant had the intent to assassinate the President is indispensable for recognizing the purpose of insurrection against him.

However, at the time of filing the original indictment, it was stated as a factual allegation that Defendant also conspired with A to assassinate the President, but this part of the indictment was later amended in the lower court, and the lower court’s factual findings also finalized that Defendant had no relation to the assassination of the President. Therefore, attempted major participation in insurrection cannot be established against Defendant. Although the record suggests some doubt that on the day of the incident Defendant may have, in the sequence of acts he performed until A was arrested, either cooperated with A’s conspiracy or aided it, that doubt arises only from inference and circumstances. Since insurrection is a crime with a specific purpose, the evidence or facts to establish that purpose are major facts requiring strict proof. Thus, the fact that Defendant did not immediately report A after the crucial shooting cannot be deemed a suspicious circumstance from which it reflexively follows that he participated in the major duties of insurrection. Especially given the situation at the time, there was no guarantee that Defendant himself would not be shot by A. To say that merely because he did not disclose A’s offense until four hours after the assassination, when reporting to the Minister of National Defense and the Army Chief of Staff, he did so for the purpose of insurrection is a leap in logic. Moreover, in this case, where no one can deny that A’s attempt at insurrection failed because of Defendant’s report, it is not proper under the principle of fairness to infer from the reporting fact a basis unfavorable to the Defendant and thereby convict him.

Therefore, as to Defendant C, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that would maintain the lower judgment, which does not establish the several decisive circumstances set forth above. The grounds of appeal on these points are meritorious.

(2) As to Defendants E and F

The lower judgment finding these Defendants guilty of attempted insurrection and murder with insurrectionary purpose also cannot be left standing. It is undeniable that, as co-defendants and subordinates of D, they shot and killed U and X, security guards of the Presidential Security Service, while staying at the Gungjeong-dong intelligence restaurant on the day of the offense. However, for that act to be murder with insurrectionary purpose, there must be awareness of the insurrectionary purpose, namely subversion of the Constitution. On this point, the only materials the lower court or the majority opinion regarded as evidence are the statements the Defendants made during the military investigation. Their statements merely amount to saying they thought that if things went well, they would be promoted or get a share. To say that those statement entries are sufficient evidence that they knew of subversion of the Constitution, i.e. the assassination of the President, and participated in the offense exceeds the bounds of free conviction.

As to how those statements were made, the record shows they were the result of leading questions and inferences made by the military investigative authorities, so one cannot distinguish whether they are opinions or statements of fact. It is hard to understand how they can be linked to awareness of the assassination of the President or subversion of the Constitution. Regarding the circumstances by which the Defendants came to shoot, co-defendant D merely instructed them to “drive the security guards in the restaurant into a corner and, if they resist, return fire.” Defendant F was D’s driver, and E was also a guard at Gungjeong-dong with little education. Even if one has difficulty asking them about the meaning of subverting the Constitution, the minimum would be awareness of the assassination of the President. Yet there is no clear material in this case showing even that awareness on their part. To uphold a death sentence by recognizing that all of this existed is unacceptable.

(3) As to Defendant G

This Defendant is recognized by the lower court as having committed attempted insurrection and murder with insurrectionary purpose by carrying out so-called confirmation killing 30 minutes after the gunfire in this case, thereby completely extinguishing the lives of T and U, who were still alive at the time. This part also cannot be left standing.

The time of the above confirmation killing by the Defendant is fixed by the lower court as 20:05 on that day, whereas the shooting of Chief T by A was at 19:40. Then it is difficult, in view of the various materials, to conclude that even 25 to 30 minutes after the first shot T was still groaning and had not died. On that day A shot T, then fired at the President, and shortly thereafter hid in the restroom, then fired the final shot into T’s abdomen and again shot the President; the record and the lower court both accept this. Then T’s time of death would have been at least before, or at the same time as, the President’s death. The hospital authorities stated that the President’s time of death was five minutes before the time the body was transported to the military hospital, that is, before 19:57 that day. In the end, if the President’s time of death can be estimated as 10 to 12 minutes after A’s first shooting, then T’s time of death would also be 19:50 or 19:52. Then it would be reasonable to conclude that at the time of Defendant G’s confirmation killing at 20:05, the victim T had already died. Otherwise, because the autopsy report and photographs of the body are in the record and the exact location of the gunshot wounds is clearly shown, the court should have had an expert assess the time of death and conducted a hearing accordingly.

Nevertheless, without taking such measures, to recognize murder with insurrectionary purpose and even impose the death penalty merely on the Defendant’s statement that T seemed to be making some sound at the time of the confirmation killing is utterly incomprehensible. Therefore, failing to examine this point and determine whether it was murder or merely a gunshot at a corpse amounts to a failure of hearing or defect for lack of reasons. Moreover, the record does not show where or what the Defendant was doing before the confirmation killing. To recognize guilt for insurrection on the ground that the killing was for an insurrectionary purpose is also not free from the criticism of finding facts without evidence.

For these reasons, I cannot agree with the majority opinion that would maintain the Army High Military Court judgment on Defendants C, E, F, and G, and I state that the grounds of appeal on these points are meritorious.

위증죄에서 말하는 false statement라는 것은 그 objective fact가 false라는 것이 아니라 스스로 체험한 fact를 memory에 반하여 statement하여 즉 memory에 반하는 사실을 말하는 것인바, 일건 record에 의하면 피고인은 시종 criminal intent를 부인하고 있을 뿐만 아니라 이 사건 complainant 이월분에 대한 judicial police officer 작성의 statement record 및 이월분 작성의 statement의 각 기재에 의하더라도 위 이월분 자신도 그와 위 조보경간에는 계금, teahouse management에 관한 transaction relations 외에도 보관금 등의 transaction relations가 있어서 보관금중 165,200원을 계금에 불입시켜 deduct하고 나머지 34,800원을 조보경에 준일이 있다(다만 보관금을 200,000원이라고 주장하고 따라서 위 165,200원을 deduct하여 remainder가 34,800원이라고 하여 보관금과 지급금이 각기 100,000원의 차이가 있다.)고 말하고 있어 이월분은 조보경과의 다방 partnership 사실을 부인하고 조보경을 다방 madam으로 고용한 것이라고 하여 partnership funds조로 700,000원을 받은 사실이 없다고 부인하고 있기는 하나 이와 같은 transaction과는 separate하게 조보경에게 돌려주어야 할 보관금이 있어 이중 165,200원을 deduct한 나머지 money를 돌려주었다고 하는 것이니 피고인의 testimony가 위와 같은 facts에 비추어 memory에 반하는 false statement라고 단정할 수 없다고 할 것이며 그 밖에 피고인의 testimony가 memory에 반하는 false statement라고 인정할만한 evidence를 가려낼 수가 없으므로 사실심으로서는 피고인의 criminal intent를 인정하려면 first 위 조보경, 이월분간의 various transaction relations를 좀더 심리하여 피고인의 testimony가 전연 터무니 없는 것인가의 여부를 가렸어야 할 것임에도 불구하고 이와 같은 점에 대한 심리를 다하지 아니한 채 이월분이 주장하는 objective facts에도 상당부분이 들어맞는 testimony를 false statement라고 판시하였음은 결국 위증죄의 legal principle을 오해하여 심리를 다하지 아니하고 채증법칙에 위반하여 facts를 오해한 잘못을 저질렀다고 할 것이다.
상고논지는 그 reason이 있다.
그러므로 원심판결을 reverse하고, 원심으로 하여금 다시 심리판단케 하기 위하여 사건을 서울형사지방법원 collegial division에 remand하기로 관여법관의 의견이 일치하여 주문과 같이 판결한다."}

{"[88DO650]": "Defendants들의 상고이유와 국선변호인의 상고이유를 together 판단한다.
원심이 인용한 제1심판결이 채택한 evidence에 의하여, court below는 피고인 <삭제>이 평소 피해자 <삭제>이 약간 저능아인 동피고인의 처에게 젖을 달라는 등의 희롱을 하는데 심한 불만을 품어 오던 중 1987. 8. 8. 23:30경 충북 괴산군 <삭제>구판장에서 피해자와 술을 마시다가 위 구판장 주인 공소외 <삭제>으로부터 그날 낮에도 피해자가 동피고인의 처에게 젖을 달라고 희롱하였다는 말을 듣고 피해자의 뺨을 수회 때리는 등의 구타를 한 후 그곳에 찾아온 피고인 <삭제>와 피해자 등 셋이서 술을 더 마시기 위하여 함께 인근 <삭제>으로 가던 중 위 마을 앞 농로상에 이르렀을 때 술에 만취된 피해자가 손가락으로 눈을 뺄 것 같은 시늉을 하면서 이새끼 까불면 죽인다는 등의 욕설을 하자 피고인 <삭제>은 손바닥으로 피해자의 뺨을 수회 때리고 피고인 <삭제>는 피해자의 복부를 2회 때려 피해자를 넘어뜨린 다음 순간적으로 분노가 폭발하여 피해자를 살해하기로 마음먹고 피고인 <삭제>은 피해자의 배 위에 올라타 가로 20센티미터, 세로 10센티미터의 돌맹이 (증제1호)로 피해자의 가슴을 2회 내려치고, 피고인 <삭제>도 이에 합세하여 가로 13센티미터, 세로 7센티미터의 돌맹이 (증제2호)로 피해자의 머리를 2회 내려친 후 다시 피해자를 일으켜 세워 피고인 <삭제>가 피해자의 복부를 1회 때려 뒤로 넘어지게 하여 피해자가 뇌진탕 등으로 인하여 정신을 잃고 축 늘어지자 그가 죽은 것으로 오인하고 그 사체를 몰래 파묻어 증거를 인멸할 목적으로 피해자를 그곳에서부터 약 150미터 떨어진 개울가로 끌고 가 삽으로 웅덩이를 파고 피해자를 매장하여 피해자로 하여금 질식하여 사망에 이르게 한 사실을 인정하고 있는바, 기록에 대조하여 살펴보면 위 인정은 정당하고 거기에 논지가 주장하는 바와 같은 체증법칙을 위배하여 사실을 오인한 위법이 없으며, 또한 사실관계가 위와 같이 피해자가 피고인들이 살해의 의도로 행한 구타 행위에 의하여 직접 사망한 것이 아니라 죄적을 인멸할 목적으로 행한 매장행위에 의하여 사망하게 되었다 하더라도 전 과정을 개괄적으로 보면 피해자의 살해라는 처음에 예견된 사실이 결국은 실현된 것으로서 피고인들은 살인죄의 죄책을 면할 수 없다 할 것이므로 같은 취지에서 피고인들을 살인죄로 의율한 제1심판결을 유지한 원심의 조치는 정당하고 거기에 아무런 잘못도 없다.
또한 record에 의하면 피고인 <삭제>이 위 범행 당시 다소 음주한 상태에 있었던 사실은 인정되나, 그로 인하여 동 피고인이 심신미약의 정도에까지 이른 것으로는 보여지지 아니하므으 이 점에 관한 소론 주장도 이유 없다.
그리고 징역 10년 미만의 형이 선고된 이 사건에 있어서 원심의 sentencing이 과중하다는 주장은 형사소송법 제383조 제4호 규정에 비추어 적법한 상고이유가 될 수 없다. 논지는 모두 이유 없다.
그러므로, 피고인들의 상고를 모두 기각하고, 상고 후의 구금일수 중 일부씩을 본형에 각 산입하기 하여 관여법관의 일치된 의견으로 주문과 같이 판결한다.
1988. 6. 28."}
