Thus, based only on such vague assumptions, it is difficult to justify measures that seriously restrict freedom of the person, such as “detention without any upper limit on duration.” One cannot conclude that a foreigner who has committed a crime in the Republic of Korea will abscond or commit crimes again if released from detention. Moreover, among persons subject to deportation there may be not only foreigners who have committed crimes and been sentenced to punishment, but also foreigners who have merely violated administrative regulations concerning entry or stay. Detaining all such persons without any time limit on the premise that they are potential fugitives or potential criminals is an excessive measure.

As for cases where the detainee files a cancellation action against the deportation order or applies for refugee status recognition, etc., institutional improvements such as having the courts give priority and focus to such cases and expediting refugee status examination and decisions can minimize instances in which the detention period exceeds the upper limit. Even if detention is released after exceeding the upper limit, it appears possible to prevent flight or additional unlawful acts to a considerable extent through measures such as restricting their residence until departure requirements are met or requiring periodic reporting of residence, designating a guarantor or requiring the payment of an appropriate security deposit, and continuously observing and supervising them through supervisors, etc. Therefore, it is doubtful that, in order to achieve the legislative purpose of the 심판대상조항, one must necessarily adopt a method that excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person, such as detention without any upper limit on duration.

3) It is difficult to regard foreigners who were apprehended and detained because they did not choose voluntary departure for various reasons or because voluntary departure was impossible as having, in effect, a “freedom to depart,” so the infringement of fundamental rights due to the absence of an upper limit on detention period cannot be deemed mitigated on the ground that persons subject to deportation have the freedom to depart at any time and thus escape from being detainees (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Jeong-mi, Kim I-su, Lee Jin-seong, and Kang Il-won in Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2013HEONBA196).

The detainee may request temporary release from detention from the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office (hereinafter referred to as the “head, etc.”); however, unless there are circumstances such as a successful cancellation action against the deportation order, etc., whether to grant temporary release from detention is entirely within the discretion of the head, etc., so the temporary release from detention system cannot be regarded as substantially functioning as a device that can supplement the problem of long-term detention. Other ex post remedies such as objections to deportation orders and detention orders likewise cannot be regarded as effective, as will be discussed below.

4) In this way, although the public interest the 심판대상조항 seeks to achieve is significant and detention of persons subject to deportation is necessary to achieve that public interest, even taking this into account, the degree to which the detainee’s freedom of the person is restricted by detention without any upper limit on duration is excessively large; accordingly, the 심판대상조항 fails to satisfy the requirements of minimum infringement and balance of interests.

(c) Conclusion

The 심판대상조항 infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.

(2) Whether the principle of due process is violated

Article 12(1) of the Constitution provides that “No person shall be punished, placed under preventive restrictions, or subjected to forced labor, except by law and due process,” thereby setting forth the principle of due process. Since the principle of due process applies not only to criminal procedure but to all state action (see Constitutional Court 1992. 12. 24. 92HEONGA8; Constitutional Court 2014. 8. 28. 2012HEONBA433, etc.), it must also be observed in the execution of deportation orders and detention orders carried out as part of immigration control administration.

(a) Since alien detention under the Immigration Control Act is equivalent to “체포 or 구속” in criminal procedure and deprives a foreigner of freedom of the person, there must be, even if not the strict warrant principle of a prosecutor’s request and a judge’s issuance, at least a device by which a person in an objective and neutral position other than an immigration control official can review the validity of such physical restraint (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Jeong-mi, Kim I-su, Lee Jin-seong, and Kang Il-won in Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2013HEONBA196). However, the current alien detention system under the Immigration Control Act is contrasted with detention in criminal procedure, where the commencement and extension of detention are decided by the court and the end point is also clearly prescribed, in that no third independent neutral institution or judicial body is involved at all in the stages of commencement and extension of detention.

(b) First, regarding the issuance and execution of detention orders, the deportation procedure for foreigners under the Immigration Control Act is structured such that ① immigration control officials apprehend and investigate suspects (Article 47 of the Act), ② the head, etc. issues a detention order and immigration control officials execute it (Article 51(1), Article 53, detention for the determination of deportation), ③ the head, etc. examines and decides whether to deport, then issues a deportation order and detention order (Article 58, Article 59(2) and (3), the 심판대상조항, Article 78(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act), and ④ immigration control officials execute them (Article 62(1), Article 63(6), Article 53, detention for the execution of deportation). Accordingly, although, formally, the investigation procedure and the review procedure are separated and the entity issuing the detention order and the executing agency are separated, in reality subordinates and superiors within the immigration office together conduct suspect investigations and issue and execute deportation orders and detention orders. In other words, the head, etc., who makes the detention decision is not an independent third institution but merely a superior within the same executing agency to which the immigration control officials belong, so the institutions cannot substantively be said to be separated, and because there is no room for external institutions such as the judiciary to intervene, it is difficult to say that procedural control by an objective and neutral institution is achieved merely by having decisions made by a superior in the same executing agency (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Jeong-mi, Kim I-su, Lee Jin-seong, and Kang Il-won in Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2013HEONBA196).

Although the 심판대상조항 is phrased as a permissive clause stating that a person “may be detained,” in practice, when a deportation order is issued, detention orders are issued simultaneously with or immediately after the deportation order, without any special review of the detention order itself such as the necessity of detention or the risk of flight, and there has been no case in which a detention order was not issued for a person subject to deportation who could not be immediately repatriated. However, because a person subject to deportation cannot always be deemed to be at risk of flight, a separate determination of the necessity of detention is required, and unless a neutral institution capable of ensuring fairness and objectivity intervenes, the current structure in which a detention order is issued almost automatically upon a deportation order is unlikely to change.

By way of reference, in Germany, both pre-deportation detention for examination of deportation and secured detention for execution of deportation are subject to a judge-issued warrant requirement, so judicial control is exercised from the commencement stage of detention.

(c) Regarding ex post remedies or control procedures, the detainee may file an objection with the Minister of Justice against a detention order or a deportation order (Article 55(1), Article 60(1) of the Act), and the head, etc. may extend detention with prior approval from the Minister of Justice where the detention period exceeds 3 months (Article 63(2) of the Act).

However, the Minister of Justice is in reality merely the supervisory authority over the administrative agency issuing and executing detention orders, and thus it cannot be said that a review system by an external neutral and objective institution is thereby secured. Indeed, there has not been a single case in the past five years (from 2013 to 2017) in which an objection against a detention order or deportation order was granted, and prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extension of detention is also almost invariably granted in reality when the head, etc. submits the application documents while deportation execution is delayed, so even from this perspective it is difficult to regard the Minister of Justice’s review and determination as having substantive significance as a control procedure to ensure the legality of detention (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Jeong-mi, Kim I-su, Lee Jin-seong, and Kang Il-won in Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2013HEONBA196).

In addition, the detainee may file an administrative action against a deportation order, detention order, or a decision dismissing an objection, but general and ex post judicial control methods such as administrative litigation are insufficient to adequately secure the freedom of the person of a foreigner who is unfamiliar with the Korean judicial system and not proficient in Korean.

(d) Since one of the important procedural requirements that can be derived from the principle of due process is to give the parties an opportunity to submit opinions and materials (see Constitutional Court 2003. 7. 24. 2001HEONGA25; Constitutional Court 2015. 9. 24. 2012HEONBA302), such opportunity must also be guaranteed to the detainee in detention under the 심판대상조항.

However, the Immigration Control Act contains no provision requiring that the person concerned be given an opportunity to submit opinions before issuance of a detention order under the 심판대상조항. Article 22(3) of the Administrative Procedures Act provides that when an administrative agency issues a disposition imposing obligations on a party or restricting rights and interests, the agency shall give the party, etc. an opportunity to submit opinions; however, “dispositions concerning the entry and departure of foreigners” are excluded from the scope of the Administrative Procedures Act (Article 3(2) No. 9 of the Administrative Procedures Act, Article 2 No. 2 of the same Act’s Enforcement Decree), and no system such as a pre-arrest judicial review of suspects exists under the Criminal Procedure Act. Therefore, the person subject to a detention order has no opportunity whatsoever to make statements or submit opinions favorable to him or her. At the stage of objection to detention, the Minister of Justice is merely authorized at his or her discretion to hear the statements of the parties concerned if necessary (Article 63(6), Article 55(3) of the Act), and prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extension of detention is also conducted only through review of documents submitted by the head, etc., without giving the detainee an opportunity to state opinions or submit materials.

(e) Considering these points together, the 심판대상조항 violates the constitutional principle of due process because there is no control procedure by a fair and neutral institution at the stages of commencement or extension of detention, and no opportunity to submit opinions is guaranteed when physical restraint is imposed administratively.

(3) Conclusion

The 심판대상조항 violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and the principle of due process, thereby infringing the detainee’s freedom of the person, and is therefore unconstitutional.

5. Conclusion

Since the 심판대상조항 is not in conformity with the Constitution, a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution shall be rendered, and the provision shall be provisionally applied until remedial legislation by the legislature is enacted, with 2025. 5. 31. as the deadline. In addition, Constitutional Court Decision 2017HEONGA29, in which the Constitutional Court had previously held, in a view different from this decision, that the 심판대상조항 does not violate the Constitution, shall be modified to the extent inconsistent with this decision. Except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Lee Eun-ae, Lee Jong-seok, and Lee Yeong-jin, the opinions of the Justices participating in this decision were unanimous, and with respect to the constitutional opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon, there is a supplementary opinion by Justice Lee Mi-seon as set forth in Section 7 below.

6. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Lee Eun-ae, Lee Jong-seok, and Lee Yeong-jin

We conclude that the 심판대상조항 does not violate the Constitution, and state our view as follows.

A. Precedent of the Constitutional Court

In Constitutional Court Decision 2017HEONGA29 rendered on 2018. 2. 22., the Constitutional Court held, for the following reasons, that the 심판대상조항 does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction or the principle of due process and therefore does not infringe freedom of the person.

“(1) Whether the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction is violated

In determining whether the 심판대상조항 infringes the freedom of the person of a person subject to deportation, it must be considered that detention under the Immigration Control Act is part of immigration control administration, which is a national administrative function, and that it is necessary for performing the functions of a sovereign state and therefore may be determined in part as a matter of legislative policy.

(a) Legitimacy of legislative purpose and appropriateness of means

The 심판대상조항 has a legitimate legislative purpose of promoting national security, maintenance of order, and public welfare by appropriately controlling and adjusting the entry, exit, and stay of foreigners. Detaining a person subject to deportation in a detention facility until departure requirements are met is an effective means for prompt and efficient execution of a deportation order and for immigration and residence management of foreigners; thus, appropriateness of means is also recognized.

(b) Minimum infringement

1) Persons subject to deportation are foreigners whose entry itself is unlawful, who violate stay conditions such as by exceeding their period of stay, or who commit unlawful acts during their stay, and who are therefore persons likely to disturb public order. As to such persons, protection and management for repatriation are necessary until they are returned to their home countries in order to ensure national security, maintenance of order, and public welfare. Therefore, detaining persons subject to deportation until the time repatriation becomes possible is a necessary measure to achieve the legislative purpose of the 심판대상조항.

2) A person subject to deportation under the 심판대상조항 is detained when immediate repatriation outside the Republic of Korea is impossible for reasons such as the absence of a passport or lack of transportation. Since the period required varies depending on each country’s circumstances and the progress of procedures, it is impossible to know in advance when repatriation will become possible. Therefore, there is an unavoidable aspect to allowing detention “until repatriation becomes possible” without setting an upper limit on the detention period.

In addition, detention under the 심판대상조항 is possible only for the purpose of securing execution of the deportation order and only for the minimum period necessary to achieve that purpose. The Supreme Court also held that detention under the 심판대상조항 has substantive and temporal limits (see Supreme Court Decision 99DA68829, decided on 2001. 10. 26.). In practice, deportation is mostly executed promptly, and the average detention period is about 11 days.

3) Since a person subject to deportation cannot stay in the Republic of Korea but can at any time leave the state of detention by voluntarily departing to his or her home country or a third country, it cannot be said without qualification that a person subject to deportation suffers serious mental pressure because he or she cannot predict when release will occur. If an upper limit on the detention period were prescribed in the 심판대상조항, detention would have to be released once the upper limit is exceeded, and if persons subject to deportation go into hiding after release, execution of the deportation order may become impossible or significantly difficult. In addition, persons subject to deportation may become involved in crime or become victims of crime, and if they remain unlawfully in the country, there is also a high likelihood that they will receive inferior treatment with respect to wages and other working conditions.

Therefore, prescribing an upper limit on the detention period in the 심판대상조항 may not only impair national security, maintenance of order, and public welfare, but may also lead to results that are by no means desirable for the human rights of persons subject to deportation.

4) Looking at the legislation of other countries, there are not a few countries that do not establish an upper limit on the period of detention for execution of deportation. The United States provides that an alien against whom a deportation order has become final must be deported within the 90-day removal period and must be detained during that period, and where the alien cannot be deported within that period and the removal period is extended, the alien may be detained during the extended period; however, the law does not provide an upper limit on the detention period after the removal period. Canada and Australia also provide that aliens may be detained for execution of deportation but do not prescribe an upper limit on the detention period, and Japan merely provides that when a person subject to deportation cannot be deported immediately, the person may be detained “until repatriation becomes possible,” without setting an upper limit on the detention period. China likewise provides only that where forced departure has been decided but cannot be executed immediately, the alien must be detained in a detention center or a place for repatriation of foreigners, without setting an upper limit on the detention period. In view of these points, if the Republic of Korea were to set an upper limit on the detention period, the possibility that the number of foreigners staying unlawfully in the Republic of Korea may sharply increase through abuse of such limit cannot be ruled out.

5) The Immigration Control Act provides various means by which a person subject to deportation may be released from detention, such as temporary release from detention (Article 65(1) and (2)), approval of extension (Article 63(2) and (3)), and objection to deportation orders and detention orders (Article 60(1) and (4), Article 63(6), Article 55(1) and (2)); furthermore, a person subject to deportation may file an administrative action seeking cancellation of a deportation order or the detention pursuant thereto or may request a stay of execution. Thus, various systems capable of releasing a person from detention under the 심판대상조항 are in place, supplementing the absence of an upper limit on the detention period.

6) Alternative legislation such as restrictions on residence, designation of a surety, or a security deposit system may be considered in place of detention under the 심판대상조항; however, unless custody of the person subject to deportation is secured, prompt execution of the deportation order and effective stay management cannot be achieved to the same extent as under the 심판대상조항, and it is difficult to conceive of a legislative alternative that achieves the legislative purpose to the same extent as the 심판대상조항 while restricting the fundamental rights of persons subject to deportation less.

(c) Balance of interests

The national security, maintenance of order, and public welfare that the 심판대상조항 seeks to protect are highly significant, and the detention system under the 심판대상조항 is indispensable to realize them. On the other hand, a person subject to deportation is only temporarily and provisionally restricted in freedom of the person until the deportation order can be executed, and various systems for release from detention are in place. Therefore, the 심판대상조항 also satisfies the balance of interests requirement.

(d) Conclusion

The 심판대상조항 does not infringe the freedom of the person of a person subject to deportation in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.

(2) Whether the principle of due process is violated

(a) In determining whether the 심판대상조항 violates the principle of due process, it must be considered that a person subject to deportation cannot stay in the Republic of Korea but can at any time leave the state of detention by voluntarily departing to his or her home country or a third country; that persons subject to deportation are normatively people who cannot stay in the Republic of Korea; and that detention under the Immigration Control Act is part of immigration control administration, which is a national administrative function, and thus may be determined in part as a matter of legislative policy.

(b) In light of the particular nature of detention of persons subject to deportation, whether the enforcement, investigation, review, and execution of deportation orders and detention should be handled by the same administrative agency, by different administrative agencies, or with judicial involvement is a matter of legislative policy. Therefore, the mere fact that no procedure is prescribed for receiving judicial determination at the stages of commencement or extension of detention does not immediately mean a violation of the principle of due process. Rather, in a specialized administrative field such as immigration control, it is also efficient for the same administrative agency to perform related tasks simultaneously, and in major countries such as the United States and Japan, the judiciary does not intervene in decisions on deportation orders and detention or in the execution of those decisions.

Meanwhile, a person subject to deportation may obtain a judicial determination on the legality of detention by filing an administrative action challenging the deportation order or detention or by filing a motion for a stay of execution of such detention; thus, it cannot be said that there is no control procedure by an objective and neutral institution.

(c) A person subject to deportation is given an opportunity to state opinions during the investigation process prior to the deportation review (Article 48(3) and (4) of the Immigration Control Act), and may state opinions or submit materials in the course of an objection to detention or administrative litigation (Article 69(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act). In addition, the Immigration Control Act provides a duty to present the detention order upon execution (Article 63(6), Article 53, Article 78(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act) and a duty to give written notice within 3 days (Article 63(6), Article 54 of the Immigration Control Act), thereby complying with the procedural requirements derived from the principle of due process.

(d) Accordingly, the 심판대상조항 cannot be regarded as violating the constitutional principle of due process.”

B. Whether there is a need to recognize a change of precedent

(1) Article 23(2) No. 2 of the Constitutional Court Act allows the Court, if supported by at least 6 Justices, to change an opinion previously expressed by the Constitutional Court regarding the interpretation or application of the Constitution or statutes. However, in order to change precedent, in addition to the formal requirement of such a qualified quorum, it must be recognized that there is a need to change the position of the precedent, for example because there is a legal error in the precedent’s reasoning or because circumstances have changed. Also, from the standpoint of foreseeability, legal stability, and the protection of trust, it must be shown that there is a need to change the position of the precedent, namely that there has been a change in normative or factual circumstances, such as changes in social institutions or culture, changes in the public’s legal sentiment or consciousness, or changes in the content of other laws or the legal principles concerning them, and that for this reason the position of the precedent must be changed (see the dissenting opinion of Justices Lee Eun-ae and Lee Jong-seok in Constitutional Court 2018. 12. 27. 2015HEONBA77 et al.).

(2) The constitutional opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon and the constitutional opinion of Justice Lee Seon-ae regarding the 심판대상조항 (hereinafter referred to as the “constitutional opinions”) held that detention without an upper limit is beyond the limits of detention as a temporary and provisional compulsory measure; that, in light of numerous foreign examples that set upper limits on detention periods, it is difficult to regard the absence of an upper limit on detention period as inevitable; that the objection system against detention orders, the Minister of Justice’s approval system for extension of detention periods, and the temporary release from detention system alone are insufficient to properly control the detention period and alleviate excessive restriction on the body; that execution of deportation orders can be secured through various alternative means such as restrictions on residence or reporting, designation of a surety, a security deposit system, or observation or supervision through supervisors; and on those grounds held that the 심판대상조항 violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction. The constitutional opinions also held that the 심판대상조항 violates the principle of due process and infringes freedom of the person because no third independent neutral institution or judicial body is involved at all at the stage of commencement or extension of detention, because the detainee is not guaranteed a procedural opportunity to state opinions and submit materials from before the issuance of the detention order through the stage of objection, and because ordinary administrative litigation procedures cannot be regarded as guaranteeing swift and effective judicial relief. However, it is doubtful whether the reasons set out in the constitutional opinions truly amount to a change in normative or factual circumstances that would justify changing the precedent.

(3) First of all, as the precedent already stated, detention under the 심판대상조항 must be imposed only for the purpose of securing execution of a deportation order, and even when detention is lawfully imposed, it may be maintained only temporarily for the minimum period necessary to achieve that purpose until repatriation becomes possible. According to the record of this case, the average detention period from the time a person subject to a deportation order completes repatriation preparations until repatriation is 10.1 days in 2018, 9.6 days in 2019, and 16.9 days in 2020. In 2020, considering that the period increased due to suspension or reduction of departure flights caused by the spread of COVID-19, the detention period appears to be on a decreasing trend compared to the time of the precedent decision; in light of this, detention under the 심판대상조항 seems in practice to be executed mostly within the substantive and temporal limits of its purpose.

Although the Immigration Control Act does not set an upper limit on the detention period, it supplements the system so that detention may be imposed only for the minimum period necessary, by allowing a person subject to deportation, if he or she objects to a detention order, to file an objection with the Minister of Justice (Article 63(6) and Article 55 of the Immigration Control Act), by requiring the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office to obtain the Minister of Justice’s approval every 3 months when detention exceeds 3 months (Article 63(2)), and by allowing the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office to temporarily release detention ex officio or upon request by the detainee, etc. (Article 65). In addition, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may release a person from detention if it becomes manifest that the person subject to deportation cannot be repatriated for reasons such as denial of entry from another country (Article 63(4)), and Article 6(2) of the Regulations on Handling Temporary Release from Detention provides that if a person requested for temporary release from detention has won at first or second instance a cancellation action against a deportation order or a decision of non-recognition of refugee status, the relevant procedure shall, in principle, be followed to permit general release or special release. Thus, as pointed out in the constitutional opinions, the possibility that the detention period may be prolonged indefinitely is not high merely because repatriation is impossible due to denial of entry from another country or because a refugee status denial decision or deportation order is being contested.

(4) Moreover, the precedent already, after a normative judgment premised on most of the factual circumstances now pointed out in the constitutional opinions, held the 심판대상조항 constitutional while pointing out the need to improve the system, and the system and practice have since been continuously improved.

(a) Expansion of the proportion of departure orders

The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office is reducing the proportion of apprehended persons admitted to detention facilities by adopting the method of issuing “departure orders based on the principle of no detention” rather than deportation orders accompanied from the outset by detention orders, with respect to foreigners with no criminal record and minors. While in 2017 the proportion of departure orders among departure measures was only 57.5%, it reached 78.3% in 2020 and 73.2% in 2021, showing that the proportion of deportation orders is decreasing and the proportion of departure orders is increasing. This confirms that the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office operates practice so that where the necessity of detention is not great, departure orders based on the principle of no detention are used as much as possible.

(b) Substantialization of the objection system

A detention order presupposes a deportation order, and if the Minister of Justice determines that an objection to a deportation order is well-founded, the suspect’s detention is immediately released (Article 60(4) of the Immigration Control Act) and the original stay status is restored, making it possible to work, etc., depending on the type of stay status; whereas even if an objection to a detention order is granted, that alone does not affect the deportation order. Therefore, from the party’s perspective, objecting to the deportation order rather than to the detention order may be a more fundamental remedy. In fact, the number of objections to detention orders was 9 in 2018, 5 in 2019, and 7 in 2020, which is markedly fewer than the number of objections to deportation orders (72 in 2018, 54 in 2019, and 67 in 2020).

It is true that, so far, no objection to a detention order has been granted, and therefore it is difficult to say that objections to detention orders themselves have become active. However, in the case of deportation orders, the grant rate for objections, which was 0% in 2016 and 2017, increased to 5% on 2018. 12. 5., 2% in 2019, and 6% in 2020; considering this trend toward substantialization of objections to deportation orders, which are the cause of detention, it cannot be categorically said that the fact that no objection to a detention order has been granted means that objections lack significance as a substantive control procedure.

(c) Expanded effectiveness of the extension approval and temporary release systems

Where detention exceeds 3 months, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office must obtain prior approval from the Minister of Justice every 3 months by demonstrating the necessity of extending the detention period (Article 63(2) of the Immigration Control Act, Article 78(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act). This approval system for extension of detention has also gradually become substantial, and the number of disapproval cases, which was only 12 in total from the introduction of the system until 2015. 8., has significantly increased to 181 in total from 2015. 9. 1. to 2021. 5. 11.

In addition, Article 4(2) of the Regulations on Handling Temporary Release from Detention, amended by Ministry of Justice Directive No. 1303 on 2020. 8. 14., provides that when reviewing temporary release from detention, primary consideration shall be given to: ① whether the person falls under a patient, pregnant woman, elderly person, minor, etc. under each item of Article 56-3(3) of the Immigration Control Act; ② whether, in light of the detainee’s health condition, it is appropriate to detain the detainee; ③ where the detainee is supporting a child under 18 years of age, whether there is anyone other than the detainee to support that child; and ④ whether repatriation outside the Republic of Korea is possible, including whether there is any reason why immediate repatriation is impossible. Moreover, temporary releases from detention, which totaled 601 cases over five years from 2013 to 2017 (an average of 120 per year), amounted to 461 cases in 2021 alone, mainly for foreigners with no criminal record, and the grant rate relative to the number of applications reached 44% in 2019, 54% in 2020, and 56% in 2021; in particular, all applications for temporary release from detention by minors in 2018 and 2019 were granted. Thus, the relevant rules have been amended, and in practice the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office actively grants applications for temporary release from detention by foreigners with no criminal record or minors, so the effectiveness of the temporary release from detention system is also expanding.

(d) As seen above, considering that since the precedent decision, positive institutional and practical improvements have been made to supplement the absence of an upper limit on the detention period, it cannot be said that there has been a change in normative or factual circumstances sufficient to justify changing the precedent.

(5) The constitutional opinions state that, in light of many foreign examples establishing an upper limit on the detention period, it is possible to set a reasonable upper limit on detention. However, in the case of the United States, the law merely provides that if a foreigner does not leave within the 90-day removal period, detention of the foreigner may continue after the removal period, and does not expressly specify a legal upper limit; and the federal regulations on detention after the removal period, enacted after the U.S. Supreme Court held in Zadvydas v. Davis that the reasonable period during which detention is possible after expiration of the 90-day removal period is presumed to be 6 months, provide only that in certain cases, such as detention for security or terrorism reasons, continued detention is possible even if deportation execution is impossible, without otherwise placing any special restriction on the detention period, as already explained in the precedent. Neighboring countries of the Republic of Korea, such as Japan and China, still do not prescribe an upper limit on the period of custody for persons subject to deportation; this circumstance is the same as at the time of the precedent decision, namely that if the Republic of Korea were to set an upper limit on the detention period, the possibility of a sharp increase in the number of foreigners staying unlawfully in the Republic of Korea cannot be ruled out.

(6) The matter of setting an upper limit on the detention period of persons subject to deportation is tied to whether there are measures to secure execution of deportation, whether there is a system to manage persons subject to deportation who are released from detention, and whether support measures for their livelihood, employment, housing, and medical care are in place. This shall be examined.

(a) Difficulty in executing deportation against persons refusing departure

Detention under the 심판대상조항 is intended to secure execution of deportation, so in order to set an upper limit on the detention period, repatriation or deportation of persons subject to deportation must first be possible within a fixed period. However, in the case of persons subject to deportation whose actions to cancel the deportation order and detention order or actions to cancel the decision of non-recognition of refugee status have all been dismissed and whose judgments have become final and conclusive, and who thereafter are refusing departure without particular reason, there is no means of forcibly deporting them other than inducing departure through interviews, persuasion through family members or acquaintances, requests to their home-country consulates for support and cooperation in deportation, and efforts to execute deportation at national expense; and even by the method of escorting the foreigner abroad together with immigration control officials, airlines may refuse boarding for security reasons, making execution difficult. Thus, if a person subject to deportation refuses departure, it is in practice impossible to execute deportation within a certain period. In fact, according to the record of this case, it is recognized that many of the persons subject to deportation who have been under long-term detention for more than one year are people refusing departure, intentionally damaging passports or even refusing a proposal that deportation be executed at national expense. In such a situation, if an upper limit on the detention period is set and detention is to be released after a certain period, there is a concern that this may greatly undermine the will of persons subject to deportation to depart voluntarily.

(b) Difficulty in managing the stay of persons subject to deportation released from detention

In order to set an upper limit on the detention period, a system capable of systematically managing persons subject to deportation who have been released from detention must be established as a premise. In order for measures such as restricting residence or requiring reporting while releasing detention due to expiration of the detention period, designating a guarantor, or requiring payment of a security deposit, to have effectiveness, the costs and material and human resources necessary for managing them must all be secured. However, it can be confirmed that, from 2018 to 2020, a total of 394 temporary releases from detention occurred, and in 60 of those cases the temporary release was revoked due to unknown whereabouts and flight. Thus, it is difficult to say that the management of foreigners temporarily released from detention is currently being carried out thoroughly. In light of this, if the number of persons subject to deportation who are released from detention increases beyond the current level by setting an upper limit on the detention period, it is doubtful whether their stay in the Republic of Korea can be managed efficiently.

Furthermore, whether to release persons subject to deportation after the upper limit on the detention period has been exceeded and whether to permit their stay in the country are closely related to national policies on employment, wages, housing, medical care, and livelihood support. For example, in Germany, where an upper limit on detention exists, a foreigner who has an obligation to depart but whose deportation is difficult for factual or legal reasons is granted Duldung, a temporary suspension of deportation execution; a foreigner granted Duldung may receive permission to work after a three-month waiting period, except in exceptional cases such as where the foreigner is at fault for the non-deportable reason, thereby establishing a system that can ease the conditions of stay for foreigners released from detention. By contrast, in the Republic of Korea, concrete support measures for housing, medical care, and livelihood for persons who have not obtained domestic stay status or whose domestic stay status has been revoked are not specifically in place; rather, in the case of temporary release from detention, conditions are sometimes attached prohibiting profit-making activities such as employment during the release period (Article 13(3) No. 4 of the Regulations on Handling Temporary Release from Detention). Thus, no system exists to ease the conditions of stay for foreigners released from detention. In such a situation, if an upper limit is set on the detention period and persons subject to deportation whose detention period has exceeded that limit are allowed to stay in the Republic of Korea, the livelihood and health of such persons may be threatened, they may become more exposed to crime, and difficulties may arise in public safety and maintenance of order.

(c) Thus, the issue of imposing an upper limit on the detention period of persons subject to deportation should be discussed on a policy basis grounded in social consensus regarding how much administrative cost arising from the management of persons subject to deportation released from detention can be borne, what employment opportunities should be granted to foreigners subject to deportation, and what level of humanitarian support should be provided. In the precedent, while noting the need to carefully examine whether a reasonable upper limit on detention suited to the circumstances of the Republic of Korea can be established, it was held that there are unavoidable aspects to not setting an upper limit on detention, taking into account that setting such a limit is not merely a matter of immigration control administration but is closely related to overall national policy. It is difficult to say that there have been policy changes or other changed circumstances that would justify altering that judgment.

(7) Whether to have a third independent neutral institution or a judicial body intervene at the stage of commencement or extension of detention is a matter of legislative policy in each country. The 심판대상조항 cannot be held to violate the principle of due process merely because the legislature excluded court involvement at the stage of commencement or extension of detention of persons subject to deportation in order to expand administrative expertise, ensure prompt response, and promote appropriate and efficient immigration control taking into account diplomatic relations and international situations. As a matter of principle, execution of a deportation order should be carried out without delay (Article 62(3) of the Immigration Control Act), and detention under the 심판대상조항 is a temporary and provisional measure taken to achieve the objective of prompt execution of a deportation order by detaining a person who cannot be repatriated immediately outside the Republic of Korea. In light of the purpose and spirit of detention under the 심판대상조항—“prompt and efficient execution of a deportation order”—it is doubtful whether making an independent and neutral third institution review and control the validity of detention at the commencement stage would be a practical measure. In addition, the Minister of Justice has established within the Ministry of Justice the “Deliberation Committee on Long-Term Detention of Foreigners,” which includes private members such as lawyers, professors, religious figures, and members of organizations related to international organizations or civic groups, to deliberate on matters concerning release from detention or temporary release from detention of foreigners detained for more than one year [Article 2(1) and (4), Article 3(1) of the Guidelines for the Operation of the Deliberation Committee on Long-Term Detention of Foreigners (as amended by Ministry of Justice Regulation No. 1250 on 2020. 4. 14.)], thereby also establishing procedures to reflect the opinions of neutral third parties in matters such as release from long-term detention.

Furthermore, because a deportation order is the premise for a detention order and detention is carried out to execute the deportation order, in determining whether the person subject to deportation was afforded a procedural opportunity to submit opinions and materials, the series of procedures from the deportation order through detention must be examined organically and comprehensively. The United States also guarantees opportunities for hearings, presentation of evidence, and examination of witnesses in deportation order proceedings conducted by immigration judges under the Department of Justice [Immigration and National Act, Sections 239 and 240], but does not grant an essential opportunity to state opinions at the stages of commencement of detention, requests to review release from detention, or applications for release from detention based on habeas corpus. Thus, at what stage and in what manner procedural rights are guaranteed from deportation order through commencement, extension, and release from detention are matters each country may determine within the scope of legislative policy. Therefore, whether the 심판대상조항 complies with the principle of due process should be determined not by whether a separate opportunity to state opinions or submit materials is granted at each stage of commencement, extension, and release of detention, but by whether an opportunity to submit opinions and materials regarding the deportation order, detention order, and release from detention is guaranteed in the overall procedure.

First, at the stage where a deportation order, which is the premise of a detention order, is made, if procedural opportunities to state opinions and submit materials are guaranteed in the investigation of a foreigner suspected of being subject to deportation, namely the suspect (Article 47 of the Immigration Control Act), and in requests to appear and interrogation (Article 48), it cannot be said that the principle of due process is violated merely because an opportunity to submit opinions and materials is not separately granted before the detention order is issued. In addition, a person detained pursuant to a detention order is immediately guaranteed an opportunity to contest the detention order through an objection to detention. In particular, because materials substantiating the grounds for the objection must be attached to the objection petition (Article 69 of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act), and because the Minister of Justice may hear the statement of the person concerned if necessary before deciding on the objection (Article 55(3) of the Immigration Control Act), it cannot be categorically said that the stage of objection completely excludes the opportunity for the party to submit opinions and materials. Furthermore, the detainee may also apply for temporary release from detention by submitting a request for temporary release accompanied by materials substantiating the grounds for the request and the ability to pay a security deposit at any time during detention (Article 65(1) of the Immigration Control Act, Article 79(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act), thereby being able to submit opinions and substantiating materials concerning temporary release from detention in writing.

In addition, the Immigration Control Act and its Enforcement Decree require that the detention order be presented upon execution (Article 53 of the Immigration Control Act); that within 3 days from the date of detention, a detention notice stating the reasons, date, and place of detention and the fact that an objection may be filed be notified to the legal representative (Article 54(1)); that if the detained person so desires, the date, place, and reasons for detention be notified to the consul of the country of nationality or citizenship stationed in the Republic of Korea, unless there are urgent circumstances or other unavoidable reasons (Article 54(2)); that a decision on an objection must be prepared in the form of a decision document stating the order, reasons, applicable provisions, etc., and sent to the applicant (Article 70(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act); and that where approval for extension of detention period is sought pursuant to Article 63(2) of the Immigration Control Act, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office must directly substantiate the necessity of extending the detention period (Article 78(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Immigration Control Act), thereby sufficiently preparing procedures to guarantee the party’s procedural rights within the bounds that do not undermine the efficiency of immigration control administration. Therefore, the 심판대상조항 cannot be deemed to violate due process merely because it does not expressly afford the detainee a procedural opportunity to submit opinions and materials at the stages of commencement or extension of detention.

(8) Meanwhile, detention under the 심판대상조항 is an administrative disposition by which a person subject to deportation is temporarily taken and confined as part of immigration control administration to secure execution of a deportation order, and the strict warrant principle under Article 12(3) of the Constitution does not apply. In addition, although Article 12(6) of the Constitution requires that a procedure be established so that not only arrest or detention in criminal procedure but also arrest or detention in administrative proceedings can be reviewed by a court as to legality, the legislature is afforded legislative discretion in shaping the concrete contents of such procedure (see Constitutional Court 2004. 3. 25. 2002HEONBA104). In particular, detention under the 심판대상조항 is carried out to ensure the administrative purpose of securing execution of a deportation order and to execute it efficiently, and its purpose and nature differ from physical restraint in criminal procedure or other administrative restraint whose very purpose is to restrict freedom of the person; thus, matters concerning its concrete procedure lie within the domain of policy discretion (see Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2003HEONMA87; Constitutional Court 2014. 4. 24. 2011HEONMA474 et al.). Therefore, as already stated by the Constitutional Court in its 2014. 8. 28. 2012HEONMA686 decision, a person subject to deportation may not only contest the causal relationship by filing a cancellation action against the deportation order that gave rise to the detention, but may also file an administrative action seeking cancellation of the detention order itself or apply for a stay of execution thereof; and, as noted above, strict prior procedures such as presentation of the detention order upon execution, written notice of the date, place, and reasons for detention, as well as ex post relief measures such as objections to the detention order in addition to objections to the deportation order, are in place, effectively supplementing the limitations of remedies through administrative litigation procedures. Since the legislature’s judgment cannot be said to exceed the scope of legislative discretion, the 심판대상조항 does not violate Article 12(6) of the Constitution. In addition, for the same reason, we dissent from Justice Lee Mi-seon’s constitutional opinion in the form of a supplementary opinion, which held that the 심판대상조항 violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution, in addition to the five Justices’ constitutional opinion of incompatibility with the Constitution.

(9) Taking the foregoing into account, the points raised in the constitutional opinions cannot be said to constitute changed circumstances sufficient to alter the precedent, and no other necessity for changing the Constitutional Court’s precedent is recognized.

C. Conclusion

Since the Constitutional Court stated in its 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29 decision that the 심판대상조항 does not violate the Constitution, the normative or factual circumstances surrounding the 심판대상조항 do not appear to have changed so drastically as to require a stricter determination than before regarding whether the provision is unconstitutional, and no other new necessity for reinterpretation can be found. Rather, the Ministry of Justice, the competent ministry, has continuously improved the relevant systems and practices since the above 2017HEONGA29 decision was rendered. Considering that immigration control administration is an area in which legislative policy is determined to a certain extent, there remains doubt whether it is desirable, after only about 5 years, to change the precedent and thereby eliminate through a Constitutional Court decision the room for voluntary and gradual institutional improvement by the legislative and executive branches.

The precedent’s position that the 심판대상조항, which is established to conduct immigration control administration as a sovereign state, does not violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction or the principle of due process remains valid even at this time, there is no error in that judgment, and no necessary and sufficient changed circumstances justifying a change of precedent can otherwise be recognized.

Accordingly, the 심판대상조항 does not violate the Constitution.

7. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Lee Mi-seon to the Constitutional Opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon

In addition to the constitutional opinion of the five Justices that the 심판대상조항 violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and the principle of due process, I wish to state as follows that it also violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution, which provides for the right to request judicial review of the legality of arrest or detention.

Article 12(6) of the Constitution provides: “Any person arrested or detained shall have the right to request a court to review the legality of the arrest or detention.” Thus, it establishes the system of judicial review of arrest or detention. This is an ex post remedial procedure intended to promote prompt and effective relief by allowing a person whose freedom of the person has been restricted by arrest or detention by public power to request judicial review by a court, and to obtain immediate release not only where the physical restraint was unlawfully commenced but also where continuation of the restraint is unlawful.

Because the freedom of the person guaranteed by Article 12 of the Constitution may be directly restricted not only by investigative agencies but also by other state institutions, including general administrative agencies, “arrest or detention” in Article 12(6) of the Constitution must also be interpreted broadly. Therefore, Article 12(6) applies to all cases in which any public power exercising agency restricts freedom of the person by means of arrest or detention. Furthermore, Article 12(6) is a provision that guarantees at the constitutional level a procedure by which the person concerned may request a court to review the legality of the arrest or detention itself, separate from the final judicial determination procedure regarding the causal relationship that led to the arrest or detention. Because this right to request judicial review of arrest or detention has an independent status at the constitutional level, the legislature has an obligation to provide persons concerned, through the overall legal system, with at least one opportunity to properly exercise the concrete procedural right (see Constitutional Court 2004. 3. 25. 2002HEONBA104; Constitutional Court 2014. 8. 28. 2012HEONMA686). Furthermore, Article 12(6) of the Constitution states that “any person” has the right to request a court to review the legality of arrest or detention, thereby recognizing that right also for foreigners.

Accordingly, with respect to a foreigner detained pursuant to the 심판대상조항, there must be provided at least one opportunity to request judicial review of the legality of the detention itself (see Constitutional Court 2014. 8. 28. 2012HEONMA686).

However, the 심판대상조항 and the Immigration Control Act, including the 심판대상조항, do not establish a procedure by which, in the event of detention pursuant to the 심판대상조항, the legality of the commencement or continuation of detention may be requested to a court for review. In addition, the Habeas Corpus Act, which provides for court remedies concerning bodily liberty, excludes “persons detained pursuant to the Immigration Control Act” from the scope of its application (see Article 2 and Article 3 of the Habeas Corpus Act), so foreigners detained pursuant to the 심판대상조항 cannot, unlike other forms of administrative physical restraint, file a petition for relief under the Habeas Corpus Act.

In shaping the procedure for realizing the right to request judicial review of arrest or detention, the legislature has relatively broad legislative power and may make various choices regarding the concrete contents and nomenclature of the law in the course of legislation (see Constitutional Court 2004. 3. 25. 2002HEONBA104), and the detainee may file an administrative action seeking cancellation of the detention order or a motion for a stay of execution thereof. However, the purpose of guaranteeing the right to request judicial review of arrest or detention separately from the right to file a judicial action under Article 27(1) of the Constitution is to enable a person who has been physically restrained by public power to request judicial review of the legality of the commencement or continuation of the physical restraint, thereby establishing a prompt and effective remedy. Yet, in the current situation where no court involvement whatsoever exists at the stage of commencement or extension of detention under the Immigration Control Act, it is difficult to say that such ordinary administrative litigation procedures alone guarantee a swift and effective judicial remedy. Also, even where detention was lawfully commenced but continuation of detention became unlawful due to the disappearance of the necessity for detention, it cannot be said with certainty whether proper and effective relief can be provided in an action to cancel the detention order or in a motion for a stay of execution. The Immigration Control Act provides an ex post remedy by allowing an objection to detention to be filed with the Minister of Justice; however, it is obvious that such an objection system cannot constitute part of the system of judicial review of arrest or detention under Article 12(6) of the Constitution, the core element of which is court review. Furthermore, ex post control by the Minister of Justice, who is merely a supervisory authority rather than a neutral and objective institution, or other procedures prescribed by the Immigration Control Act, such as prior approval by the Minister of Justice for extension of detention, presentation of the detention order to the person concerned, and detention notices, cannot be regarded as supplementing the system of judicial review of arrest or detention.

As noted above, the legislature has relatively broad legislative power in shaping the procedure for realizing the right to request judicial review of arrest or detention, but considering the purpose of Article 12(6) of the Constitution in guaranteeing that right, a procedure must be secured whereby the legality of the state of detention itself under the 심판대상조항 may be requested to a court for review; and this is equally true even if detention under the 심판대상조항 is carried out as part of immigration control administration, because the detention causes a serious restriction on freedom of the person.

Taken together, the 심판대상조항, which does not establish a procedure for requesting judicial review of the legality of the commencement or continuation of detention from a court in the event of detention under the 심판대상조항, violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution."}
